catalog_quote: There are two degrees of stress in Misantla Totonac: primary and secondary. Secondary stress falls on all heavy syllables. Heavy syllables are defined as having either a final consonant or a long vowel nucleus. Primary stress is the right-most stress in a word and is characterized as being stronger than all other cases of stress. Primary stress may fall on either a heavy or a light syllable. ... The domain of primary stress is the phonological word. ... On verbs, primary stress falls on the last syllable, whether that syllable is light or heavy. ... The assignment of primary stress on nouns differs from that on verbs. Stress generally falls on the penult when a word final syllable is light (2), and on the final syllable when a word final syllable is heavy (3). ... A word-final syllable closed by a coronal obstruent [-son, +cor] is considered light by the primary stress rule and is not stressed (4). A final syllable closed by any other segment is considered heavy by the rule therefore stressed (5). ... As on verbs, a final syllable containing a long vowel is regarded as heavy and is therefore stressed even if it is closed by a coronal obstruent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two degrees of stress. Secondary stress on every heavy syllable (closed syllable or long vowel); primary stress is the rightmost stress in the phonological word. Nouns: primary stress on the final syllable if it is heavy (long vowel, or closed by anything other than a coronal obstruent), otherwise on the penult; final CV and CVC-with-coronal-obstruent syllables count as light/extrametrical. Verbs: primary stress on the final syllable regardless of weight, except that word-final inflectional suffixes (-tat 2SUB.PL, -wa 1SUB.PL, -na 2OBJ, -la(ɬ) PFV, -ti 2PFV) are extrametrical and never stressed, so perfective verbs surface with penultimate stress; the imperfective suffix -yaa is always stressed. MacKay unifies both as 'stress the final non-extrametrical syllable' (p. 114 rule (7); p. 127-128 rule (65)).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 111: 'Secondary stress falls on all heavy syllables. Heavy syllables are defined as having either a final consonant or a long vowel nucleus.' p. 112 fn. 4: 'Secondary stress will not be marked in the transcription as it is predictable and falls on every heavy syllable.'
new_statements.exceptions: pp. 114-115: (1) some noun-final CVVC syllables closed by a coronal obstruent are unstressed (lexically extrametrical, e.g. /min-cikiL-Vt/ 'your breast', /min-kii-swaat/ 'your molar'; stress returns when a suffix follows); (2) a few final CVC-coronal nouns are stressed ([θatát] 'soft', [časás] 'white'); (3) [tamín] 'pot' (underlying /tamink/) has unstressed final nasal syllable. Verbs: word-final inflectional suffixes never stressed (Levy p.c. reports the same for Papantla); reduced [-n] of -na 2OBJ and [-w] of -wa 1SUB.PL do end up stressed on the ultima; /-kan/ REFL always stressed (treated as derivational). A word-final syllable ending in /n/ is always stressed (p. 127).
new_statements.domain_note: p. 112: 'The domain of primary stress is the phonological word. All clitics are lexically stressed and do not affect the assignment of primary stress (e. g. /štan/ PAST).' Forms cited with pronouns in phrase context; data from the Yecuatla and San Marcos Atexquilapan (SM) variants of Misantla Totonac (fn. 10, 12).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog yecu1235 'Yecuatla Totonac' is the same language as MacKay's 'Misantla Totonac' (ISO 639-3 tlc; Glottolog lists MacKay's Misantla grammars under this code). MacKay 1992 states its data come from the Yecuatla variety (fn. 10: perfective suffix full form [-laɬ] 'in Yecuatla, Veracruz') with some forms marked (SM) from San Marcos Atexquilapan (fn. 12); the encyclopedia snippet confirms 'Data on Misantla Totonac come from Yecuatla and San Marcos Atexquilapan'. No separate glottocode for the San Marcos variant.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same rule as the existing MacKay 1992 statement (verbs final; nouns penult if final light, final if final heavy) and adds the extrametricality analysis and the secondary-stress-on-heavy-syllables rule; the catalog record itself has an empty rule field, which these statements fill as weight-sensitive.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Same system as MacKay 1992: nouns take penultimate stress when the final syllable is light and final stress when the final syllable is heavy (CVV or CVC, with a final syllable closed by a coronal obstruent counting as light); verbs take final stress, since all inflectional suffixes are extrametrical; analysed as final stress plus extrametricality of word-final light syllables, with primary stress the rightmost stress of the word.

new_statements.identity_note: Both MacKay works describe the Yecuatla variety of Misantla Totonac (the only surviving variety, per the earlier-saved Wikipedia text and WALS 'Totonac (Misantla)' = tlc / yecu1235). No other dialect is described.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same rule as the catalog source (MacKay 1992: heavy = long vowel or closed; primary = rightmost stress; verbs final, nouns penult if final light else final). The 1994 sketch adds that secondary stress also falls on the word-initial syllable and restates the coronal-obstruent lightness condition; nothing differs in placement or type.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two degrees of stress. Secondary stress on the word-initial syllable and on every heavy syllable (CVV or CVC). Primary stress is the rightmost stress in the word: on verbs it is final; on nominals it is final unless the final syllable is light (CV, or CVC closed by a coronal obstruent), in which case it is penultimate. Stress is predictable, so lexical stress is (almost entirely) unnecessary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of the word and on all heavy (CVV, CVC) syllables; the first syllable is said to receive a 'very strong secondary stress' (snippet near p. 409).
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final CVC closed by a coronal obstruent [-son, +cor] counts as light for primary stress on nominals (snippet: 'Final CV or CVC|[-son +cor] syllables are not..'); 'almost all' cases need no lexical stress (snippet), implying a small residue of lexically stressed items.
new_statements.identity_note: MacKay 1994 describes Misantla Totonac as spoken in Yecuatla (YEC) and San Marcos Atesquilapan (SM), Veracruz (snippet: 'is based on data from the towns of Yecuatla (YEC) and San Marcos Atesquilapan (SM), Veracruz'), i.e. the Yecuatla variety that Glottolog codes yecu1235.
